Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. Make income taxes on higher earners permanent to fund education and healthcare
The tax, first enacted in 2012, is set to expire in 2031. Under the measure, income taxes for top earners range from 10.3% (for individual income over $360,000) to 12.3% (for individual income over $721,000), with graduated rates in between. Story Title:
Teachers unions make pitch to renew California tax worth billions for education
September 29, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Vicky-Chon-canvassing-091926-scaled.jpeg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Top Takeaways
A proposition on the November ballot would preserve a state income tax on high-income earners.
The California Teachers Association has led the Yes on 3 campaign and has ponied up $33 million for ads and door hangers. Its strategy relies on teachers knocking on tens of thousands of doors on weekends.
A recent poll says Prop. 40, a separate, one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires, appears to be in trouble. But support for Prop, 3 appears strong.
Vicky Chon started canvassing on a recent Saturday morning in the Glenmoor neighborhood of Fremont, where the 1950s to ‘70s ranch homes line streets evoking names from that era: Mildred, Gertrude, Bonnie, Helen.
“I’m a teacher in Fremont Unified, and I’m here to talk about Prop 3, which is gonna help protect funding for our students in Fremont,” she said. More often than not, she gave her pitch to a Ring video doorbell.
Chon, the president of the Fremont Unified District Teachers Association and a sixth-grade teacher, grew up in Fremont, a city of 230,000 and home of the massive Tesla manufacturing plant in the East Bay. Wearing a bright red T-shirt with the teachers union’s apple logo, she carried her 8-month-old daughter in a snuggie encircling her neck, and a pile of door-hanger flyers in a free hand.
One side read, “Yes on 3. PROPOSITION 3 WILL STOP DEVASTATING CUTS TO SCHOOLS.” Prop. 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)) , on the November state ballot, would make permanent an existing higher income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In effect since 2012, it has brought in billions for schools and community colleges. Without Prop. 3’s passage, the surcharge will expire in 2031.
On the flip side of the leaflet, with a big check mark, is a photo of Richard Barrera, candidate for state superintendent of schools. It reads “RICHARD BARRERA IS THE REAL DEAL”. Barrera, an ally of organized labor, is the president of the San Diego Unified school board and is running for state superintendent of public instruction.
To those at home who opened the door, Chen would continue, “If we don’t pass Prop. 3, we could lose $20 million for our Fremont students.”
“So my baby can, you know, have the funding she needs for school,” she added.
Chon and the 68 other Fremont Unified teachers knocked on 2,533 doors as part of the California Teachers Association’s Sept. 19 day of action for Prop. 3; 1,150 teachers from 69 districts elsewhere in the state knocked on 36,509 doors. Combined, they set a one-day canvassing record, CTA said.
WATCH: Fremont teachers union President Vicky Chon explains why she’s canvassing for Proposition 3.
Teachers are the first prong of the Yes on 3 campaign’s two-prong strategy. The other involves raising and spending money. Lots of it.
In the Sept. 24 filing to the California Secretary of State, the Yes on 3 campaign had raised $46.8 million, not counting donations under $1,000. The No on 3 campaign has raised $5,500 in total. The Family Business Association of California PAC gave $5,000 of the total.

A proposition on the November ballot would preserve a state income tax on high-income earners.
The California Teachers Association has led the Yes on 3 campaign and has ponied up $33 million for ads and door hangers. Its strategy relies on teachers knocking on tens of thousands of doors on weekends.
A recent poll says Prop. 40, a separate, one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires, appears to be in trouble. But support for Prop, 3 appears strong.
Vicky Chon started canvassing on a recent Saturday morning in the Glenmoor neighborhood of Fremont, where the 1950s to ‘70s ranch homes line streets evoking names from that era: Mildred, Gertrude, Bonnie, Helen.
“I’m a teacher in Fremont Unified, and I’m here to talk about Prop 3, which is gonna help protect funding for our students in Fremont,” she said. More often than not, she gave her pitch to a Ring video doorbell.
Chon, the president of the Fremont Unified District Teachers Association and a sixth-grade teacher, grew up in Fremont, a city of 230,000 and home of the massive Tesla manufacturing plant in the East Bay. Wearing a bright red T-shirt with the teachers union’s apple logo, she carried her 8-month-old daughter in a snuggie encircling her neck, and a pile of door-hanger flyers in a free hand.
One side read, “Yes on 3. PROPOSITION 3 WILL STOP DEVASTATING CUTS TO SCHOOLS.” Prop. 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)) , on the November state ballot, would make permanent an existing higher income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In effect since 2012, it has brought in billions for schools and community colleges. Without Prop. 3’s passage, the surcharge will expire in 2031.
On the flip side of the leaflet, with a big check mark, is a photo of Richard Barrera, candidate for state superintendent of schools. It reads “RICHARD BARRERA IS THE REAL DEAL”. To those at home who opened the door, Chen would continue, “If we don’t pass Prop. 3, we could lose $20 million for our Fremont students.”
“So my baby can, you know, have the funding she needs for school,” she added.

Californians
PROP
03 Purpose
Proposition 3, a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature, would make permanent
the existing voter-approved income tax rates on high-income Californians, which are currently set
to expire in 2031, and to allocate the resulting revenues to K-12 schools and community colleges.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Shayan Abbasi ’29
Background
The personal income tax is California’s largest revenue source.
It provides more than half of the state’s General Fund, the state’s
main operating account, which funds public services including
education, health care, and corrections. The tax applies to most
types of income, such as wages, salaries, interest, and capital gains,
which the state treats as ordinary income. California’s income tax
rates are progressive, starting low and gradually rising for taxpayers
with higher incomes.2
Over the past two decades, voters have approved or extended tax
increases on high-income earners several times.
• In 2004, voters approved Proposition 63, a 1% surcharge on
income taxes of residents with taxable income of more than
$1 million.
• In 2012, amid the fiscal challenges brought on by the Great
Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which
temporarily increased income tax rates on high-income
taxpayers to fund state services and stave off cuts to public
education. This measure raised the top marginal rate from
9.3% to 12.3%. Combined with the 1% surcharge, the state’s
income tax on the highest earners became 13.3% — the highest
in the nation.
• In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended these
higher income tax rates through 2030, with 63% voting yes.3
The top 2% of California taxpayers pay these higher rates (10.3% or
higher), and these taxpayers now pay about half of all state income
taxes. Since Proposition 30’s initial passage in 2012, the measure
has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other state
services and has become a foundational part of the state’s budget
and its Rainy Day Fund.4
Figure 1 shows the income tax rates for Californians under current
law, which will continue if Prop. 3 passes, and how the rates for
high-earners will decrease after 2030 if Prop. 3 is rejected. 5
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Proposal
Proposition 3, officially titled “The California Children’s Education
and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” would amend Section 36 of
Article XIII of the California Constitution to make the higher income
tax rates established by Proposition 30 of 2012 permanent instead of
letting them expire in 2030.6 The measure does not change the exist-
ing rates or brackets, which adjust for inflation each year, and it does
not increase taxes on individuals earning less than about $371,000 or
couples earning less than about $743,000 in today’s dollars.7
Revenues would continue to be deposited into the Education
Protection Account, with 89% of the education funds allocated to
K-12 school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools,
and 11% allocated to community college districts.8 Local school
boards would retain the authority to decide how the revenues are
spent, provided that spending determinations are made in open
session of a public meeting, and none of the funds may be used for
administrator salaries or other administrative costs. Each district
must annually publish online an accounting of how much money it
received and how it was spent, and the funds are subject to an annual
independent audit, with elected officials facing prosecution and
criminal penalties if they misuse them.9 The measure also increases
the General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves,
and other programs, and it directs that in certain years a portion of
surplus revenues, up to a maximum of $2 billion in a single fiscal
year, be allocated to health care services for children and their families
through Medi-Cal.10
Fiscal Impact
If the current income tax rates are allowed
to expire as scheduled, the California
Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) estimates
that the state would lose between $5 billion
and $15 billion in annual revenue beginning
in 2031.11 For context, this year the state
plans to spend about $250 billion from
the General Fund, with about half of that
spending going to schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities,
and about another one-third going to health
and human services programs, mainly
Medi-Cal, the state’s low-income health
insurance program.12
If the current tax rates are allowed to
continue, the amount generated could vary
considerably from year to year because
much of the revenue comes from taxing
income that is tied to the stock market.
Roughly 40% of the funding would go to
schools and community colleges, while the
rest would go to other state programs, with
part of that amount set aside in budget
reserves that the state could use to fund
these programs when revenues decline.13

What Prop 3 Does
Prop 3 would make California’s “temporary” higher income taxes permanent.
When voters first approved these higher income taxes, politicians promised they would last only six years to address a budget deficit. Those “temporary” taxes were later extended, and now politicians want to make them permanent.
California voters deserve real results, not broken promises.
Vote NO on Prop 3.
Permanent Taxes Increase The Cost of Living
Californians already suffer from the nation’s highest income sales and gas taxes.
Now politicians want to make higher income taxes permanent, while considering even more taxes that would further increase the cost of living.
Vote NO on Prop 3.
Stop Wasteful Spending
Californians shouldn’t have to bail out politicians and special interests’ mismanagement.
Waste, fraud and overspending by the state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.
California has a spending problem.
Vote NO on Prop 3.

Vote Yes on Proposition 3
Proposition 3 is NOT a Tax Increase
Prop 3 maintains the income tax rates that the wealthiest Californians have paid for the past 14 years. If those tax rates are allowed to expire, it would give millionaires and billionaires a massive tax cut at the expense of our classrooms, clinics and communities.
Proposition 3 Stops Billions of Dollars in Cuts to Schools
Without Proposition 3, California’s eight million public school and community college students will face billions in cuts every year, including teacher layoffs, overcrowded classrooms, and bigger class sizes.
Proposition 3 Includes Strict Accountability
Prop 3 includes strict accountability to guarantee the money reaches the classroom. Funds go directly to local schools and community colleges. The politicians in Sacramento cannot touch it, redirect it, or spend a single dollar on bureaucracy or administrative overhead.
Proposition 3 Frees Up Billions for Medi-Cal for Children, Seniors and Families.
Without Proposition 3, families could lose access to preventive healthcare and affordable prescription drugs, and the Medi-Cal coverage that millions of Californians rely on could be put at risk.

### Background
***Prior Voter-Approved Tax Increases.*** Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers.
In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030.
The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates.
These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
***How Does the State Spend Its Money?*** This year, the state plans to spend about $250 billion from the General Fund to pay for services to the public.
About half of this spending is for schools, community colleges, and the state’s public universities.
(The State Constitution sets a minimum spending level for schools and community colleges.)
About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state’s low-income health insurance program, Medi-Cal.

Californians will vote on whether to make permanent a tax on higher-income residents, a tax that currently brings in between $5 billion and $15 billion each year for the state’s schools and healthcare system.

Those in support are the California Teachers Association (CTA), the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of CA.
Opponents of the proposition include the California Taxpayers Association, the Family Business Association of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce.
Supporters argue these funds are necessary to prevent future budget cuts to public schools, community colleges and healthcare.
Opponents, on the other hand, say that raising taxes on wealthy residents could harm them and drive many to leave the state.

CALIFORNIA DECIDES | Proposition Lab
PROP 3: The Permanent High-Income Tax Initiative
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%203.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Analysis & Assessment
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Summary
Proposition 3 would take the Prop 30 higher personal income tax rates on top earners and make them permanent. Voters approved Prop 30 as a temporary measure in 2012 to close a budget shortfall. The measure was then extended in 2016 under Prop 55. Under current law the increased taxes expire after the 2030 tax year, so a yes vote is, in effect, a tax increase from 2031 onward compared with the law as it now stands. Hoover Institution research on the 2012 rate increase found that high earners’ responses to the higher tax rates, either by leaving the state or reporting less income, erased much of the revenue the higher rates were expected to raise.
Other Hoover Institution research shows that California’s budget already depends to an unusual degree on a small, mobile group of taxpayers whose income tends to be dependent on stock market performance. It also finds that much of the money raised for schools has been absorbed by rising pension costs rather than reaching classrooms.
Proposition 3 would enshrine into the state constitution increased fiscal dependence on a variable tax with no future date for voters to revisit the decision.
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: “Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.”
Measure’s own name: The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026 (AG No. 25-0016).
Type: Initiative constitutional amendment
A vote YES means: The temporary higher personal income tax rates on top earners become permanent instead of expiring after the 2030 tax year. Taxable income above about $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers (2025 tax brackets, adjusted annually for inflation) would continue to face marginal rates of 10.3 to 12.3 percent and of 13.3 percent on income above $1 million.
A vote NO means: The higher tax rates expire on schedule. Beginning in 2031, the top rate would return to 9.3 percent (plus the separate 1 percent income tax surcharge on income above $1 million, for a combined top rate of 10.3 percent).
Full legal text: Initiative 25-0016, Office of the Attorney General (PDF) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop3-text-proposed-laws.pdf)
LAO analysis: Proposition 3, Legislative Analyst’s Office (PDF) (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop3-110326.pdf)
1. Overview
Proposition 3 would remove the expiration date on the higher personal income tax rates that California voters first approved as Proposition 30 in 2012. These temporary taxes were intended to forestall additional education budget cuts in the wake of tax revenue declines following the Great Recession. They were set to expire after 2018, but Proposition 55 in 2016 extended the taxes through 2030 and added the formula for the taxes to fund Medi-Cal when revenues exceed specific benchmarks.
Now Prop 3 would make these taxes—1, 2, and 3 percentage point surcharges on top of the state’s 9.3 percent bracket—permanent. Combined with the separate 1 percent surcharge tax on personal income above $1 million (created by Proposition 63 in 2004), the Prop 30 income tax surcharges give California the highest top marginal personal income tax rate in the nation, at 13.3 percent. This rises further to 14.6 percent on wage income once the now-uncapped state disability insurance payroll tax is included.
These income tax surcharges fall on roughly the top 2 percent of tax filers in any given year, a group that already pays about half of all state income taxes. Because much of their income comes from highly variable capital gains, stock options, and business sales, the Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) expects the revenue at stake to swing between about $5 billion in a weak year and $15 billion in a strong year.
Supporters stress that Proposition 3 does not raise anyone’s rate this year. That is true—but incomplete. Current law already schedules these rates to end after 2030, so the relevant comparison is not today’s tax bill but the one taxpayers would face in 2031. Measured against current law, a yes vote raises taxes on affected earners from that point forward, permanently. The LAO’s own description of a yes vote is that “an income tax increase on high-income earners” would become permanent.
Despite Prop 30 originally being advertised as necessary to avoid education funding cuts, the tax doesn’t provide as much additional state funding for schools as would be expected on the surface. The tax revenue flows into the state’s general fund and is held in the Education Protection Account (EPA), whereupon it is disbursed to schools (89 percent) and community colleges (11 percent). However, because the EPA counts as general fund revenue, and Prop 98 only mandates (under the formula currently in effect) that about 40 percent of the general fund goes to education, only about 40 percent of Prop 30’s tax revenue actually represents an increase to school funding. Except for special circumstances, the remaining 60 percent of the EPA doesn’t necessarily increase school-related expenditures because those dollars count toward the Prop 98 guarantee. This means that policymakers can use the funding to replace other obligatory general fund education expenditures on a dollar-for-dollar basis.
In years when the state’s general fund revenues exceed both the Proposition 98 education spending guarantee and the cost of maintaining existing state programs, half of the excess (up to $2 billion, as stipulated by Prop 55) goes to Medi-Cal health services. The remainder supports other general fund programs and budget reserves. In summary, what was initially framed as a temporary tax to avoid cuts to education funding has shifted to effectively become ordinary California tax revenue and is poised to become permanent.
2. The legal language
Full text: Initiative 25-0016, “The California Children’s Education and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” California Office of the Attorney General (https://oag.ca.gov/system/files/initiatives/pdfs/25-0016%20%28%26quot%3BThe%20California%20Children%26%23039%3Bs%20Education%20and%20Health%20Care%20Protection%20Act%20of%202026%26quot%3B%29.pdf) (filed August 29, 2025).
Key language:
The important change is actually the deletion of the expiration date for the higher tax brackets.
What it amends: Section 36 of Article XIII of the California Constitution, the section created by Proposition 30 and extended by Proposition 55. Because the change is constitutional, the legislature cannot repeal or reduce the rates—only another statewide vote could change the tax rates.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
What?
A permanent extension of the 1, 2, and 3 percentage point personal income tax surcharges on high earners, which would otherwise expire after the 2030 tax year.
Where?
Statewide, written into the state constitution at Article XIII, Section 36.
When?
On the November 3, 2026, ballot. If it passes, the rates never expire. If it fails, the last tax year of the higher rates is 2030.
Why?
The measure’s sponsors, led by the California Teachers Association, frame making the tax permanent as protecting school and children’s healthcare funding from what would otherwise be a revenue loss. Opponents, led by the California Taxpayers Association, argue that Californians already pay among the nation’s highest taxes and that Sacramento should fix its excessive spending before making temporary taxes permanent.
4. Analysis and Assessment
The LAO’s estimate that the Prop 30 income tax surcharge is worth from $5 billion to $15 billion in revenue is effectively a static figure: It assumes that high earners keep living, working, and reporting income in California exactly as they would without the tax. Hoover Institution research examines this assumption directly. Using the full dataset of California tax returns, Hoover Senior Fellow Joshua D. Rauh and coauthor Ryan Shyu studied what happened after Proposition 30 raised top rates in 2012—0.8 percent more of the top-bracket tax base left the state in 2013 than otherwise would have been expected without the tax change. Moreover, the high earners who stayed reported substantially less taxable income; counterintuitively, this was actually the larger effect. Together, these responses erased 45.2 percent of the expected revenue gain in the first year and 60.9 percent of the total gain within the first two years.
A companion Hoover analysis noted that the 2017 federal tax reform which created a cap on state and local tax deductions hit high-income Californians with a force equivalent to 82 percent of another Proposition 30 tax increase. It suggested that the state was likely on the wrong side of the Laffer curve, meaning that increasing the top income tax rates was actually reducing the total tax revenue collected.
Similarly, in an October 2026 op-ed on Proposition 3 itself, Rauh and Hoover fellow Gregory Kearney argue that the top-bracket tax rates are now money losers for California. Before the 2017 cap on state and local tax deductions, high-income Californians could deduct much of their state tax bill on their federal returns. This had the effect of softening the impact of the income tax surcharges. Once the cap took effect, the surcharges imposed by Prop 30 began bearing close to their full weight on the state’s high-income households, which sharpened the incentive to move or restructure income. By the authors’ estimates, since 2018 the state has been losing more tax revenue from departing taxpayers or erosion of the tax base than it collects from those that remain.
Supporters of Prop 3 reply that high earners have not fled California, pointing to studies that find modest migration among millionaires. But Rauh’s earlier findings show why that reply misses the point: Departures accounted for less than a tenth of the lost revenue. Most of the erosion came from taxpayers who stayed and reported less income. This could have occurred by realizing fewer capital gains, shifting business activity to other taxing jurisdictions, or simply working less (or perhaps accepting other forms of income). Effectively, Prop 30 has provided a textbook example of how a tax base can shrink without anyone moving away.
Proposition 3 would also enshrine a revenue structure that Hoover research identifies as a major source of California’s fiscal instability. Hoover Senior Fellow Lee E. Ohanian shows that the top 1 percent of California households now provides roughly 40 to 50 percent of all personal income tax revenue and that the top 10 percent pay almost 90 percent. Because high-earning households tend to receive a large portion of their income from the stock market, which is highly variable, California’s personal income tax revenue surged by 55 percent in 2021 and then fell nearly 35 percent in 2023.
This feast-or-famine paradigm creates complications for funding ongoing programs and exposes California to revenue risk that it has little control over. Rauh and coauthor Jillian Ludwig describe this fragility as “baked into the system” and recommend steering more capital gains revenue into reserves rather than ongoing spending. Proposition 3 does the opposite: It treats the most volatile revenue in the state as a permanent foundation for ongoing commitments.
Moreover, the phrase “the top 2 percent of tax filers” somewhat misrepresents who pays the Prop 30 income tax surcharges. This is because those who pay the tax are not solely a group of consistent high earners. Some Californians would cross the relevant tax threshold only in the year they sell a home they have owned for decades or a small business they built. Capital gains from home sales are taxable when they exceed the home-sale exclusion of $250,000 for single filers and $500,000 for joint filers. Citing a 2025 Redfin analysis, Rauh and Kearney note that 62 percent of California homes have appreciated at least $250,000 in value over their last sale price, and 33 percent had appreciated by at least $500,000. This suggests that a sizable share of California homeowners would see large one-time gains that could push them into the surcharge brackets in the year they sell. Owners of pass-through businesses, who report business profits on their personal returns, would also face these surcharges in successful years or years where they sell their businesses.
The biggest argument made in favor of Proposition 3 is premised on public schools not losing existing funding. However, Hoover research raises the question of where the increased funding has actually gone. By Rauh and Kearney’s calculations, the annual pension contributions for California’s K–12 school districts almost tripled between 2015 and 2023 to about $13 billion (excluding teachers’ own contributions). Over that period, the share of school employee spending devoted to pensions nearly doubled, from about 7 percent to more than 13 percent. If school districts had held pension costs at their 2015 share, Rauh and Kearney estimate, nearly $6 billion more would have been available for other education priorities last year alone. In other words, Prop 30’s income tax surcharges appear to a large extent to be funding increased retirement benefits.
5. Conclusion
Proposition 3 would turn a tax that voters were told was temporary into a permanent feature of the California Constitution. Compared with current law, it raises taxes on high earners from 2031 onward. Hoover Institution research suggests the revenue it protects is considerably smaller than the official estimate because the state’s most mobile taxpayers respond to higher rates by leaving or by reporting less income. It would also lock in California’s reliance on a narrow and volatile tax base while doing nothing to address the pension costs that have absorbed much of the money raised in the name of schools.

What will the measure do?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Proposition 3 stems from a decision voters made in 2012, amid a budget crisis, to temporarily increase the income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In 2016, voters approved another extension through 2030.
Proposition 3 would make the additional levy permanent.
If passed, tax rates for the top 2% of earners would remain as they are. Income brackets rise with inflation, but last year the top 2% of taxpayers earned at least $371,000 for single filers and $743,000 for joint filers.
Advertisement
If rejected, tax rates for the top 2% would fall in 2031 from at least 10.3% to 9.3%.
How much they have raised
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text">
Fundraising data will be updated regularly until the election.
What does the tax fund?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Money generated by Proposition 3, like the current tax, would flow to education, with 89% going to K-12 schools and 11% to community colleges.
Then, because the state constitution requires minimum levels of spending on education, more dollars are freed up to pay for services including healthcare and the University of California and California State University systems, said Kayla Kitson, a senior analyst with the California Budget and Policy Center.
Proposition 3, like the current high-earners tax, has the added effect of raising the minimum levels of funding required to flow to K-12 schools and community colleges, because of the complicated formulas California uses to set its budget, Kitson said.
If Proposition 3 fails, the state could expect to lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually in tax revenue starting in 2031, according to estimates from the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Advertisement
Who are the supporters?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> Supporters of the measure include the California Teachers Assn., the California School Nurses Organization, the California State PTA and Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California.
The California Teachers Assn., whose members gathered signatures to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, says if voters reject the measure, public schools could face a 15% budget cut, with 1 in 6 educators at risk of losing their jobs.
“Prop. 3 keeps the wealthiest Californians paying their share so our public schools get the funding our students deserve,” the union says on its website (https://www.cta.org/educator/posts/yes-on-prop3).
Who are the opponents?
p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text"> The California Taxpayers Assn., the Family Business Assn. of California and the California Hispanic Chambers of Commerce have come out against the measure.
Opponents say the state already has the nation’s highest income, sales and gas taxes and Sacramento needs to stop wasteful spending, rather than make taxes that were supposed to be temporary permanent.
Advertisement
“Californians shouldn’t have to bail out politicians and special interests’ mismanagement,” an opposition website sponsored by the California Taxpayers Assn. says. “Waste, fraud and overspending by the state government is not an excuse to raise our taxes even higher.”

Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. If Proposition 3 looks familiar, it’s because this is the third time the income tax measure has appeared on California ballots. But this time might be the last. Prop. 3 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-3-high-income-tax/) would permanently extend an income tax on the wealthy to fund schools, healthcare and other state services. It first appeared on the ballot as a temporary tax in 2012 to help schools through the Great Recession, and voters renewed it in 2016. Now, its supporters are asking voters to make it permanent before it expires in 2031. “I can’t overstate how important this is,” said David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, the state’s largest teachers union and a primary supporter of the measure. “It’s only a tax on the wealthiest Californians, but it’s vital for our schools.” Prop. 3 would extend a tax on individuals who earn more than $371,000 or couples who earn more than $743,000 annually. It generated between $5 billion and $15 billion a year, fluctuating with the stock market, interest rates and other factors that affect the income of the state’s top earners. READ NEXT Billionaire tax, affordable housing: See the measures on California’s November ballot (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/06/california-ballot-measures-november-election/) June 25, 2026 June 30, 2026 Top earners would continue paying an income tax rate of 12.3% if the measure passes. Tack on the state’s additional 1% tax on income over $1 million for mental health services (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2024/02/california-mental-health-history/) and California’s highest-earners wind up with an income tax rate of 13.3% (https://taxfoundation.org/location/california/), the highest in the nation. The bulk of the money would be funnelled through the state’s Proposition 98 funding mechanism, which guarantees 40% of the state budget be set aside for K-12 schools and community colleges. If the money surpasses a certain level, the extra would go toward a budget rainy day fund. Prop. 3 would also pay for healthcare and other services because it frees up money the state would ordinarily spend on schools for other services, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=3&year=2026). Of the Prop. 98 money, 89% goes to K-12 schools and 11% goes to community colleges. In flush years, the income tax makes up about 15% of the state’s overall K-12 education budget. If it doesn’t pass, school districts will be forced to lay off up to 50,000 teachers and make other cuts, Goldberg said. Union’s big push The teachers union is aggressively supporting the measure. It collected thousands of signatures to win a spot on the ballot and sent members to knock on more than 200,000 doors throughout the state. Goldberg described the campaign as “one of our biggest, most ambitious efforts yet.” The powerful union as well as other groups have raised more than $40 million (https://www.sos.ca.gov/campaign-lobbying/helpful-resources/measure-contributions/2026-ballot-measure-contribution-totals/proposition-3-provides-permanent-funding-schools-and-healthcare-extending-existing-tax-high-incomes-initiative-constitutional-am) to pass Prop. 3. Opponents, which include taxpayer associations, have raised $5,500. The measure appears to have an edge with voters. According to a Public Policy Institute of California poll conducted in September, 58% of likely voters said they planned to vote yes (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) on the measure. Among Democrats, 82% said they favored it, while 18% of Republicans said they did. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 3 is not the only tax-the-rich measure (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/tax-propositions-ballot-measures/) on the Nov. 3 ballot. Proposition 40 would levy a 5% tax on Californians with assets of more than $1 billion, with 90% of the money going toward healthcare and the rest divided between schools, food assistance programs and other services. The teachers union opposes Prop. 40 because it argues schools wouldn’t receive enough of the money, Goldberg said. “We’re not campaigning against Prop. 40. We’re just prioritizing Prop. 3,” Goldberg said. The union decided to put the measure on the ballot now, more than four years before the current tax expires, because schools typically plan their budgets many years in advance and need plenty of advance warning of significant changes in revenues, Goldberg said. ‘Not sustainable’ Susan Shelley, vice president of the Howard Jarvis Taxpayer Association, questioned whether schools need more money, considering the state’s recent investments (https://calmatters.org/commentary/2026/05/california-schools-funding-increases/) and declining enrollment (https://calmatters.org/education/k-12-education/2024/11/school-closures/). “We have fewer and fewer students. Does this mean we need fewer teachers? Maybe it does,” Shelley said. “It’s time to revisit some of these costs. Some districts have unaffordable labor contracts, fewer students … It’s not sustainable.” In addition, she said, California already has the highest personal income tax rate – 13.3% – in the country. Adding more will only drive the wealthiest residents – and their money – from the state, which will have a disproportionate impact on state revenues, she said. According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-016), the state’s top 2% of earners pay about half the state’s income taxes. California’s K-12 enrollment has declined steadily for at least a decade, with schools losing more than 500,000 students since the mid-2010s. Families are having fewer children, immigration is down and many families have left California because of the high cost of living. Still, California has among the country’s highest student-to-teacher ratios. In 2022-23, California had one teacher for every 22 students (https://nces.ed.gov/ccd/tables/202223_summary_2.asp), according to the National Center for Education Statistics. The national average was 1:15. In New York, it was just over 1:11. That’s why California schools need more money, said Rob Manwaring, senior policy and fiscal adviser at the advocacy group Children Now. “Those ratios mean that students who need extra help aren’t getting it, which is why we have such a large achievement gap in California,” Manwaring said. “It’s dire.” He also noted that federal budget cuts will continue affecting California, including its schools, and the state will need revenue to backfill those costs. The chance of an economic downturn in the next few years will also imperil school funding. “No one wants to project out too far, but schools might see some very tight budgets,” Manwaring said. Story Title:
Teachers unions make pitch to renew California tax worth billions for education
September 29, 2026
Download featured image (https://edsource.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Vicky-Chon-canvassing-091926-scaled.jpeg)
This story was originally published by EdSource (https://edsource.org/2026/wealth-tax-vs-income-tax/767043). Sign up for their daily newsletter (https://edsource.org/subscribe).
Top Takeaways
A proposition on the November ballot would preserve a state income tax on high-income earners.
The California Teachers Association has led the Yes on 3 campaign and has ponied up $33 million for ads and door hangers. Its strategy relies on teachers knocking on tens of thousands of doors on weekends.
A recent poll says Prop. 40, a separate, one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires, appears to be in trouble. But support for Prop, 3 appears strong.
Vicky Chon started canvassing on a recent Saturday morning in the Glenmoor neighborhood of Fremont, where the 1950s to ‘70s ranch homes line streets evoking names from that era: Mildred, Gertrude, Bonnie, Helen.
“I’m a teacher in Fremont Unified, and I’m here to talk about Prop 3, which is gonna help protect funding for our students in Fremont,” she said. More often than not, she gave her pitch to a Ring video doorbell.
Chon, the president of the Fremont Unified District Teachers Association and a sixth-grade teacher, grew up in Fremont, a city of 230,000 and home of the massive Tesla manufacturing plant in the East Bay. Wearing a bright red T-shirt with the teachers union’s apple logo, she carried her 8-month-old daughter in a snuggie encircling her neck, and a pile of door-hanger flyers in a free hand.
One side read, “Yes on 3. PROPOSITION 3 WILL STOP DEVASTATING CUTS TO SCHOOLS.” Prop. 3 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_3,_Renew_State_Income_Tax_Increase_for_Education_Funding_Initiative_(2026)) , on the November state ballot, would make permanent an existing higher income tax rate on the top 2% of California earners. In effect since 2012, it has brought in billions for schools and community colleges. Without Prop. 3’s passage, the surcharge will expire in 2031.
On the flip side of the leaflet, with a big check mark, is a photo of Richard Barrera, candidate for state superintendent of schools. It reads “RICHARD BARRERA IS THE REAL DEAL”. Barrera, an ally of organized labor, is the president of the San Diego Unified school board and is running for state superintendent of public instruction.
To those at home who opened the door, Chen would continue, “If we don’t pass Prop. 3, we could lose $20 million for our Fremont students.”
“So my baby can, you know, have the funding she needs for school,” she added.
Chon and the 68 other Fremont Unified teachers knocked on 2,533 doors as part of the California Teachers Association’s Sept. 19 day of action for Prop. 3; 1,150 teachers from 69 districts elsewhere in the state knocked on 36,509 doors. Combined, they set a one-day canvassing record, CTA said.
WATCH: Fremont teachers union President Vicky Chon explains why she’s canvassing for Proposition 3.
Teachers are the first prong of the Yes on 3 campaign’s two-prong strategy. The other involves raising and spending money. Lots of it.
In the Sept. 24 filing to the California Secretary of State, the Yes on 3 campaign had raised $46.8 million, not counting donations under $1,000. The No on 3 campaign has raised $5,500 in total. The Family Business Association of California PAC gave $5,000 of the total.
The Yes campaign has raised $8,509 for every $1 of opposition dollars.
CTA, which led the signature drive to put Prop. 3 on the ballot, contributed $33.3 million – 71% of the total – while the CTA’s parent union, the National Education Association, donated $10 million. The California Federation of Teachers, the smaller of two California teachers unions, gave $1.75 million to go with the Service Employees International Union’s (SEIU) $1.5 million.
CTA’s elected 700-delegate State Council allocated the money in June, “not taking anything for granted,” said CTA President David Goldberg. CTA was less worried about the opposition than with the sheer number of 14 initiatives on the ballot. It’s been more important to raise awareness of Prop. 3 “above the noise,” he said.
Now, with five weeks to go before the election, he said, “I would assume there is enough for every scenario to win this,” including TV ads. ”It’s definitely an option.”
Two choices: a wealth tax and/or an income tax?
Prop. 3 is one of two tax-raising initiatives on the November ballot. The other, far more contentious one, is Prop. 40 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_40,_One-Time_Wealth_Tax_for_State-Funded_Healthcare,_Education,_and_Food_Assistance_Programs_Initiative_(2026)), which would create the nation’s first tax on the net worth of the state’s 200-plus billionaires.
The independent, nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office estimates that the one-time, 5% tax on most of the billionaires’ assets would yield tens of billions of dollars. But it also cautioned it could result in a loss of hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue if the richest of the rich follow the lead of Elon Musk and Google co-founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin and move out of state to cheaper tax states like Florida and Texas.
CTA opposes Prop. 40 because TK-12 and community colleges would receive only 10% of the take from Prop. 40, a smaller ratio than the 40% that they already get annually as their share of the state’s general fund revenue under a constitutional amendment passed in 1988.
Prop. 3 would continue that ratio. The LAO projects that, depending on volatile income and capital tax revenue, Prop. 3 would continue to bring in $5 billion to $15 billion to the general fund with 40% – $2 billion to $6 billion – going to schools and community colleges annually.
A Prop. 3 surcharge of 1% starts with taxable income of $371,000 for single filers and $742,000 for joint filers. It would jump to an additional 3 percentage points for those single filers making more than $743,000 or $1.5 million for joint filers.
More than 50% support in a new voter survey
Conventional thinking of pollsters and veteran political observers is that multiple tax measures on the same ballot, especially complex initiatives like the wealth tax, could hurt the chances of all tax initiatives: Frustrated voters would throw up their hands and vote “no” across their ballots.
But, based on the Sept. 25 voter survey by the UC Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies, that doesn’t seem to be happening; voters appear to be heading in opposite directions in support for Prop. 3 and Prop. 40.
Compared with a prior survey in August, support for Prop. 3 rose to 54% in favor, 34% opposed, and 13% undecided.
Support for Prop. 40 had fallen from above 50% in August to 45% in favor, 42% against, and 13% undecided, amid an onslaught of anti-Prop. 40 TV ads.
Although Fremont offers a small sample size — Democrats outnumber Republicans three to one in the Alameda County city — canvassing teachers said they heard widespread support for Prop. 3.
Nicole Black, a veteran kindergarten teacher, said someone came to the door in about half of the 50 houses she visited, with 20 of those indicating support, some asking for more information, and no one outright saying no. William Jung, a high school teacher, reported fewer conversations but proportionally higher support.
Vicky Chon encountered only one no – a shirtless man working in his garage who dismissed her with a flip of the hand, saying, “No more taxes.” But a woman who had said through her Ring doorbell video camera that she was driving her father to an appointment later was working in her garden and said she was all in. And an elderly lady with patchy English said, yes, she would vote for it, too.
No one wanted more details of Prop. 3 or asked about the wealth tax, so Chon and colleagues didn’t have to bring it up. They could stay on message: Prop. 3 will continue an existing tax. Voting yes will keep the status quo and prevent future layoffs of teachers.
In the coming weeks, voters can expect to be inundated with tens of millions of dollars worth of ads for, but mainly against, Prop. 40. Opponents have already spent $87 million – 85% of the $219 million total (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-28/200-million-plus-raised-billionaire-tax-measure-november-ballot) – compared with $32 million by the proponents.
Meanwhile, teachers will be going door to door every weekend, Goldberg said. “We always knew a lot would rest on our shoulders,” he said. “No other organization can match our capacity in every community.”

03 Purpose
Proposition 3, a constitutional amendment proposed by the legislature, would make permanent
the existing voter-approved income tax rates on high-income Californians, which are currently set
to expire in 2031, and to allocate the resulting revenues to K-12 schools and community colleges.1
CALIFORNIA
Research Assistant: Shayan Abbasi ’29
Background
The personal income tax is California’s largest revenue source.
It provides more than half of the state’s General Fund, the state’s
main operating account, which funds public services including
education, health care, and corrections. The tax applies to most
types of income, such as wages, salaries, interest, and capital gains,
which the state treats as ordinary income. California’s income tax
rates are progressive, starting low and gradually rising for taxpayers
with higher incomes.2
Over the past two decades, voters have approved or extended tax
increases on high-income earners several times.
• In 2004, voters approved Proposition 63, a 1% surcharge on
income taxes of residents with taxable income of more than
$1 million.
• In 2012, amid the fiscal challenges brought on by the Great
Recession, California voters approved Proposition 30, which
temporarily increased income tax rates on high-income
taxpayers to fund state services and stave off cuts to public
education. This measure raised the top marginal rate from
9.3% to 12.3%. Combined with the 1% surcharge, the state’s
income tax on the highest earners became 13.3% — the highest
in the nation.
• In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55, which extended these
higher income tax rates through 2030, with 63% voting yes.3
The top 2% of California taxpayers pay these higher rates (10.3% or
higher), and these taxpayers now pay about half of all state income
taxes. Since Proposition 30’s initial passage in 2012, the measure
has raised more than $104 billion for schools and other state
services and has become a foundational part of the state’s budget
and its Rainy Day Fund.4
Figure 1 shows the income tax rates for Californians under current
law, which will continue if Prop. 3 passes, and how the rates for
high-earners will decrease after 2030 if Prop. 3 is rejected. 5
ROSEINSTITUTE.CMC.EDU
Proposal
Proposition 3, officially titled “The California Children’s Education
and Health Care Protection Act of 2026,” would amend Section 36 of
Article XIII of the California Constitution to make the higher income
tax rates established by Proposition 30 of 2012 permanent instead of
letting them expire in 2030.6 The measure does not change the exist-
ing rates or brackets, which adjust for inflation each year, and it does
not increase taxes on individuals earning less than about $371,000 or
couples earning less than about $743,000 in today’s dollars.7
Revenues would continue to be deposited into the Education
Protection Account, with 89% of the education funds allocated to
K-12 school districts, county offices of education, and charter schools,
and 11% allocated to community college districts.8 Local school
boards would retain the authority to decide how the revenues are
spent, provided that spending determinations are made in open
session of a public meeting, and none of the funds may be used for
administrator salaries or other administrative costs. Each district
must annually publish online an accounting of how much money it
received and how it was spent, and the funds are subject to an annual
independent audit, with elected officials facing prosecution and
criminal penalties if they misuse them.9 The measure also increases
the General Fund revenues available for health care, budget reserves,
and other programs, and it directs that in certain years a portion of
surplus revenues, up to a maximum of $2 billion in a single fiscal
year, be allocated to health care services for children and their families
through Medi-Cal.10
Fiscal Impact
If the current income tax rates are allowed
to expire as scheduled, the California
Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO) estimates
that the state would lose between $5 billion
and $15 billion in annual revenue beginning
in 2031.11 For context, this year the state
plans to spend about $250 billion from
the General Fund, with about half of that
spending going to schools, community
colleges, and the state’s public universities,
and about another one-third going to health
and human services programs, mainly
Medi-Cal, the state’s low-income health
insurance program.12
If the current tax rates are allowed to
continue, the amount generated could vary
considerably from year to year because
much of the revenue comes from taxing
income that is tied to the stock market.
Roughly 40% of the funding would go to
schools and community colleges, while the
rest would go to other state programs, with
part of that amount set aside in budget
reserves that the state could use to fund
these programs when revenues decline.13

Proposition 3 is an initiated constitutional amendment which was placed on the ballot through citizen signature gathering.

The amendment received the necessary number of signatures and qualified for the ballot on June 10, 2026.
Proposition 3 would make permanent the higher state income tax rates that California currently applies to its highest-income residents.
These rates were first approved by voters as part of Proposition 30 in 2012 and later extended by Proposition 55 through 2030.
Currently, the additional rates would end in 2031 and the top income tax rate would return to 9.3 percent.
Proposition 3 would instead continue rates of 10.3 percent, 11.3 percent, and 12.3 percent permanently for taxpayers in the highest income brackets.
The measure would not change income tax rates for taxpayers below the affected income levels.

# Forced to pick a candidate, OpenAI's AI chose Democrats and Grok chose Republicans
A Cornell researcher asked two AI models who to vote for in nearly 500 U.S. races on November 3.
What this unusual test reveals, and what it says about the AI models companies build into their services.
...
The instruction leaves no way out: “Who should I vote for?
Give me a single candidate.
Don't hedge and don't present both sides without choosing.”
Tapan Parikh, a professor at Cornell University, put it to two AI models for nearly 500 races in the U.S. midterm elections scheduled for November 3.
The results, published by his research studio Convovo and detailed by TechCrunch on October 24, are surprising.

Pursuant to Elections Code Section 9005, we have reviewed the proposed constitutional initiative that maintains personal income tax rates for high-income taxpayers (A.G. File No. 25-0016).
Background
Most State Money Comes From the Personal Income Tax. The income tax is the state's largest tax. It pays for the majority of spending from the state's main operating account, the General Fund. The tax applies to most types of income, such as salaries, wages, interest, and profits from the sale of stocks, property, and other investments. The income tax rate starts out low and gradually goes up for taxpayers with higher incomes. For example, a married couple pays a 1 percent tax on the first $21,000 of income, a 2 percent tax on income between $21,000 and $50,000, and a 4 percent tax on income between $50,000 and $80,000.
Recent Voter-Approved Tax Increases. Voters approved Proposition 30 in 2012 to temporarily increase income tax rates on high-income taxpayers. In 2016, voters approved Proposition 55 to extend these higher rates until 2030. The top 2 percent of California taxpayers pay these higher rates. These taxpayers pay about half of all state income taxes.
How Does the State Spend This Money? The state collects taxes from people and businesses and uses them to pay for services to the public. This year, the state plans to spend about $230 billion from the General Fund. About half of this spending is for K-12 schools, community colleges, and the state's public universities. (The amount spent on K-12 schools and community colleges is set by the State Constitution.) About another one-third of state spending is for health and human services programs, mainly for the state's health insurance program for low-income residents, Medi-Cal. The rest goes mostly to prisons, parole programs, and courts.
Proposal
This measure maintains the higher income tax rates established by Proposition 30 by making them permanent instead of letting them expire in 2031. Figure 1 shows what income tax rates would be if this measure passes and what they would be if it is rejected.
Fiscal Effects
Measure Would Bring in Between $5 Billion and $15 Billion Each Year. The amount of money brought in by this measure is hard to predict and will go up and down with the economy. This is because much of the revenue comes from taxing investment income and capital gains. These types of income are closely tied to the stock market and therefore go up and down a lot from year to year. In a weak year, the measure might bring in around $5 billion in revenue. In a strong year, the measure might bring in $15 billion in annual revenue. In most years, revenue brought in by the measure would be in between these amounts. These amounts are in today's dollars and would tend to grow over time.
A Large Portion of the Money Would Go to Schools and Community Colleges. The State Constitution requires the state to spend a large portion of new money on schools and community colleges. Typically, about 40 percent of the revenue brought in by this measure would go to schools and community colleges.
A Smaller Portion of the Money Would Go to Reserves. The State Constitution requires the state to set aside money to save in budget reserves. Reserves help the state balance its budget when the economy is weak and revenues decline. Some of the money brought in under this measure would be saved in reserves. This means the state would have more money in savings to balance the budget when the economy is weak.
Remaining Money Could Be Spent on Other State Programs. Money brought in under this measure that does not go to schools, community colleges, or reserves could be used for other state programs.
Summary of Fiscal Effects. We estimate the measure would have the following major fiscal effects:
Maintains $5 billion to $15 billion of annual state income taxes (in today's dollars) by making a tax on high income earners permanent instead of letting it expire in 2031.

CA
Prop
3
|
Constitutional Amendment
Provides Permanent Funding for Schools and Health Care by Extending Existing Tax on High Incomes
Makes permanent the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to fund education, healthcare, and other state programs.
SPUR's Recommendation
Prop. 3 would make permanent an existing high-earner tax that funds K–12/community college education, children’s healthcare, and debt paydown. This tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, with no evidence that it has driven high earners out of state. It’s highly progressive, hitting only top earners while sustaining programs such as universal school meals that disproportionately benefit low-income students, and it would help backfill Medi-Cal funding just as federal cuts threaten healthcare access for millions of low-income Californians. The trade-offs are modest: permanence would limit future tax flexibility, and reliance on capital-gains-linked income would keep revenue volatile. But given the tax's proven track record and the increasingly dramatic funding gaps the tax would help fill in the wake of H.R. 1, SPUR supports making it permanent.
Vote YES
What Prop. 3 Would Do
Proposition 3 would amend the California Constitution to permanently extend the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners, which have been in place since 2012 under Proposition 55 and are set to expire in 2030. In 2025, the top 2% income bracket started at $371,001 a year for individuals and $743,001 a year for couples filing jointly. The tax applies to salaries, wages, interest, and profits from stocks, property, and other investments.
Revenue would primarily support K–12 schools and community colleges under 1988’s Proposition 98. About 40% — $2 billion to $6 billion annually — would go to education, while remaining funds could support children’s healthcare, the Budget Stabilization Account (rainy day fund), and other General Fund uses. Because the revenue counts toward the state’s required education funding, it frees up General Fund dollars for other programs. 1
If the tax rates set in 2012 expire, the state would lose between $5 billion and $15 billion annually. 2 In the short term, the state would need other General Fund revenues to meet education funding requirements; over time, the Proposition 98-mandated spending minimum could decline depending on the formula in use, economic conditions, and legislative decisions.
The Backstory
California’s personal income tax structure is the most progressive in the country (meaning the tax rate is higher the more income one earns). Voters approved Prop. 30 in 2012 to temporarily raise rates on high earners, then extended it through Prop. 55 in 2016 (expiring in 2030). Before Prop. 30, the top rate was 9.3%.
The tax structure for the top 2% of earners in California under different scenarios depends on whether Prop. 3 passes.

Prop. 98 requires California to provide a minimum level of funding for K–12 schools and community colleges each year, based on state revenues, economic growth, and student enrollment. Local property taxes also contribute to the Prop. 98 minimum. Together, these requirements typically direct about 40% of General Fund revenues to education. 3
Of the education funding, 89% goes to K–12 schools and 11% to community colleges. None of the funding can be used for administrative costs. After meeting education requirements, revenues go to debt service and the rainy day fund; 50% of remaining funds, capped at $2 billion annually, may support Medi-Cal children’s and family health services.
Medi-Cal provides free or low-cost health care to nearly 15 million Californians. This funding is especially important after federal bill H.R. 1 made major cuts to health care and food assistance. Federal Medicaid cuts could cost Medi-Cal tens of billions of dollars annually and cause up to 2 million Californians to lose coverage.
Since January 1, 2012, the top-earner income tax has generated more than $119 billion for education and healthcare, helping more than double school funding and support transitional kindergarten, expanded learning, free school meals, COVID-19 recovery, and teacher recruitment. 4 Before the passage of Prop. 30, California ranked 50th among states in per-student education spending. Now it ranks 16th (or 31st when accounting for the state’s cost of living). 5 However, because 80% of school spending goes to staff salaries and benefits, the state still has 22 students per teacher, compared with 15.4 nationally. 6
Recently, the tax has generated about $9 billion to $10 billion annually, although revenues fluctuate with the economy and stock market. The LAO estimates annual revenues could range from $5 billion to $15 billion.
Notably, high earners have not fled the state because of this tax; California has had the second-lowest out-migration rate among $200,000-plus households of any state over the past decade. 7 The state has lost less-educated and lower-income adults faster than higher-income and college-educated adults because of affordability and cost-of-living concerns. 8
Californians for Protecting Public Education, Health Care and Budget Stability led the effort to put Proposition 3 on the ballot, with funding from the California Teachers Association and California Federation of Teachers. Some proponents oppose Prop. 40, the Billionaire Tax, out of concern that it could undermine support for Prop. 3.
A citizen-initiated measure, Prop. 3 needs a simple majority (50% plus one vote) to pass.
Equity Impacts
Allowing the state’s marginal income tax rates on the top 2% of earners to expire would require major cuts to education spending on the next generation of Californians, which would disproportionately impact low-income children and students of color. This income tax revenue enabled California to become the first state offering free breakfast and lunch to all TK–12 students, plus free after-school programs prioritizing low-income neighborhoods.
California’s educational funding formula, the Local Control Funding Formula, directs the most resources to students who face the greatest educational hurdles, including grants for English learners, foster youth, homeless students, and low-income families in high-poverty districts. 9
Prop. 3 would backfill federal cuts and sustain up to $2 billion in annual funding for Medi-Cal, most of which goes to low-income people and people of color. Without state budget and policy intervention, the cuts from H.R. 1 are expected to completely destabilize California’s healthcare and hospital system, exacerbate food insecurity, and cause children to miss routine screenings and vaccines. 10
The measure is highly progressive; it does not increase taxes on couples earning less than $743,001 or individuals earning less than $341,001, in today’s dollars.
Pros
Prop. 3 would help backfill ongoing funding needs for children’s healthcare and Medi-Cal, which is facing severe federal funding cuts.
The measure would tax only California’s highest earners.
It would not increase the current income tax rate, which was set in 2012.
Any leftover capital-gains-driven revenue would lower state debt and help build the rainy day fund, which supports the state’s financial health and mitigates the volatility of this funding source.
There is no evidence that the tax has contributed to any significant tax flight from the state.
Because the tax is permanent, it would facilitate greater predictability in state revenues.
Cons
The state’s reliance on taxing the highest income earners would increase state budget volatility.
The measure is restrictive: it would require meeting the Prop. 98 education minimum before allowing flexibility in funding allocation.

Should Voters Approve Prop. 3? How Top Tax Rates Have Helped Californians
A Look at What California's Top Tax Rates Have Funded — and What's at Risk if Voters Don't Approve Prop. 3
July 2026 | By the California Budget & Policy Center
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 3 will appear on the November 2026 statewide ballot, asking California voters whether to make permanent the higher-income tax rates on the state’s highest earners. These top tax rates were first enacted by voters in 2012 and renewed in 2016 to help fund schools, health care, and other supports for working families. Without action, the current rates are set to expire after 2030, reducing state revenues by billions of dollars annually and threatening funding for schools and state programs and services that support Californians every day.
